This wouldn’t post earlier but I think I sorted out the problem.  
Fassbender's character is a serial murderer who kills for money and sport. "Revenge" is the excuse.  
But notice: I said "revenge \*fantasy\* film," not "revenge film” (the moral calculus of which I will discuss in a moment). The "revenge fantasy" is \*YOUR\* revenge fantasy. The revenge fantasy of the "Eat Da Rich" leftist who dreams of guillotine blades but must settle for laughing at elites getting vaporized in DIY subs, losing billions on websites and other catastrophic self-owns caused by their hubris and entitlement. We will eat cake but we will be entertained!  
"Cinephiles" have a bizarro obsession with a narrow, inflexible coulda-woulda-shoulda ruleset that films should do this or that to achieve this or that desirable effect. This approach (popularized by the Tumblr School of Critical Analysis and still followed by their immediate descendants: the BreadTube and Letterboxd/Twitter commentariat) has all the vague air of progressive intellectualism but is, in fact, a crypto-conservative doctrine. Art does not "need" to do anything. It doesn't need to dissolve nihilism, nor to promote a communitarian ethos and glorify the proletariat, nor to be morally didactic agitprop. This approach is also prone to walking face-first into the depiction/endorsement false binary as well.  
The most important sequence in the film are the scenes with the secretary. The Killer's creed includes the directive to “forbid empathy; empathy is weakness." In the van, she says, "I'm not a bad person.” Then, after a beat of silence, she almost whimpers as she says, "I'm not.” We hope for mercy. The cabbie's murder is similarly meaningless: wrong place, wrong time, wrong fare. Just another unsolved mugging-turned-murder. Casefile at the bottom of the pile.  
As for the logic of the revenge film: the protagonist's violence is justified by the ontological evil of their enemies. A failson kills John Wick's fucking dog (dogs are near-universally pure innocents in fiction; notice that The Killer does not kill The Brute's dog), and this violation gives him the green light to kill not only the son but \*everyone\* in the organization who are all complicit and fair game. The myth of economic meritocracy (wealth = hard work) is packaged with a secondary, ethical meritocracy: good things happen to good people, and bad things happen to bad people. This is a panacea. Those who find themselves in dire material straights comfort themselves that they are the meek who shall inherit the earth, and that it is harder for a rich man to get into heaven than for a camel to fit through the eye of a needle. \*The Killer\* breaks the "rules" of its genre, removing any excuse that the violence is justified or fair. The narratives of fairness in revenge films mirror the moralized narratives that justify authoritarian policies which "bad" people who are a "threat" to the divine taxpayer, from targeted criminalization of the underclass to endless "civilizational" wars. This logic is suspended for the ultra-rich, who pose more of a threat to the average taxpayer than any homeless person ever could. This is why adherence to the contemporary cinephile ruleset is a hinderance to comprehension and appreciation: it cannot accommodate intentional subversion, often ending up with inverted interpretation as a result.  
Another element of the ruleset that makes no sense is that films must be "groundbreaking." Any story told well is worth telling. This fetishization of originality and desire for novelty reeks of consumerist conditioning. Similarly, it has never been adequately justified to me why "self-evident and uncontroversial facts" should not be the so-called "point" of a film (that films need to have a “point" at all is another faulty element of the ruleset). That the police exist to protect private property of the elite class is absolutely an anti-capitalist position, and your implication it is not anti-capitalist is a confusing assertion and almost certainly unintentional on your part. "Leftists" did a lot of eye-rolling about \*Glass Onion\*, \*Triangle of Sadness\* and \*The Menu\* last year (revenge fantasies where the elites suffered humiliation and/or death), and \*Don't Look Up\* (maliciously misinterpreted as anti-populist) the year before. The artistic quality of these films is irrelevant here. This attitude of "ugh, like, I \*GET\* IT" followed by desperate searches for shaky grounds to do flaccid contrarianism is obnoxious and immature. There's no other way to describe it. A film that shares your worldview is... bad? Because it is not complex enough? Or what? When I push leftists on this, they say they “feel condescended to," or some other product of insecure projection that inevitably emerges when taste in art is reduced to a mere identity marker.   
On the topic of the commodification of identity, let's examine your assertion that, “the film’s message is actively bad almost no matter where you sit, but \*\*especially as a leftist.\*\*” Even these political labels are mere identity markers. I noticed you quoted the sentiment associated with Fisher/Zizek/Jameson that “it is easier to imagine the end of the world than the end of capitalism,” which opens Fisher's vital work, \*Capitalist Realism\*. I recommend reading Fisher’s paragraph on Kurt Cobain/Nirvana from that chapter as a supplement for this next bit.  I would quote it but it sends the post over the word count.  
The Client lives in Chicago but is styled like a pseudo-Bohemian PNW hipster who is not like The Suits, man, because he's a "cool" boss who encourages you to "express yourself" as an "individual" (trans. to consumer as a consumer). He wears a t-shirt with the logo of the "iconic" "indie" label which was initially home to Nirvana: Sub Pop. This is what Fisher was talking about: the "dreadful lassitude and objectless rage" has been appropriated by the elites who "endlessly repeat older gestures of rebellion" to self-style themselves as outsiders and underdogs. Seattle/Washington State was formerly the "grunge capital of the world" and now, as the home of Amazon and Microsoft, it is the mecca of yuppie tech gentrification. The Sub Pop t-shirt is a token that substitutes for a personality, the clothing equivalent of the "dining set that defines me as a person" that was a source of anxious rumination for Fight Club's protagonist.  
Tech billionaires produce no culture. They trade in "disruption": a set of technoutopian marketing lies about "democratization" and "freedom." Their only innovations have been (increasingly absurdist) schemes to move money from legacy corporate monopolies into corporate monopolies that they control. The Killer waits for his first target in an empty WeWork location. WeWork's "innovation" was leasing out desks in a "co-op" work environment. So... real estate. They were landlords. Their product was real estate, the most stable commodity in existence, and they went bankrupt. This must be the maverick entrepreneurial spirit I've heard such good things about.  
The film is not anti-capitalist because "dur hurr huur justice system bad." I only wrote about this (with textual support) because you have chosen to single out The Killer's decision to spare The Client as the primary strike against the film's anti-capitalist credentials. It is clear to me from all you have posted that you haven't examined what the film is communicating about The Client beyond that he is rich and does not die. Another unsupported element from the ruleset: a film's meaning is ultimately determined by its ending. Almost everything else in the film is a more interesting avenue of analysis:  
	•	The Killer's obsession with The Smiths (another example of self-identity through art consumption?)  
	•	The Killer's use of the aforementioned empty WeWork location, the tech industry's erosion of labour protections through increased numbers of atomized, non-union "gig workers." (Is The Killer a "gig worker"?)  
	•	The mass proliferation of American corporate culture across the globe post-Cold War, including the ever-presence of McDonald's.  
	•	Fincher's defenses of Netflix, a tech company which has done irreparable damage to film culture (are anti-capitalist films even possible in capitalist realism?)

I'm not German, but I was reading up a bit on censorship in Weimar Germany and it's very interesting to look at the slide into fascism and compare it to: 1. complaints made about modern art and AI art (i.e. that it's "bad" art or that it's "not art"), 2. appeals to the idea that there is "bad art" and "good art" and that the "bad art" is not only morally reprehensible but also harmful to the viewer, and 3. the current talking points of conservative politicians (i.e. "this art is bad and evil and will harm children").

>In 1907, the Kino-Debatte, or ‘film debate’ began in Germany. This was accompanied, shortly afterwards, with the Kinoreformbewegung – the film reform movement. This was a collective of bourgeois individuals who disapproved of the newfound and popular cinema, and whom subsequently pushed for greater governmental intervention on behalf of the greater public good and national morality. They were not necessarily against cinema, but instead lobbied for ‘healthy and educational films’ that would nurture strong German values and deter what they saw as the corruptive influence of the Schundfilme, or ‘trash film,’ which usually referred to foreign films. As Karen J. Kenkel indicates in her essay, “The Nationalism of the Mass Spectator in Early German Film,” the reformers, while concerned with both the quantity and quality of culturally sensitive films, were in fact more concerned with the spectators themselves.

Following the end of WWI, a brief relaxation of film censorship allowed for a slew of “Aufklarungsfilm” to hit German cinema. Aufklarungsfilm showed taboos like sex, sex work, abortion, and homosexuality. As a response, “the Leipzig boy scouts (Wandervogel) issued a manifesto disapproving of all screen trash and its promoters among the actors and owners of movie theaters...”

>That the demonstrating Dresden youth distributed anti-Semitic leaflets reveals this local campaign to have been a reactionary maneuver calculated to turn the resentments of the suffering petty bourgeoisie away from the old ruling class. By making the Jews responsible for the sex films, the wire-pullers in Dresden could be fairly sure to influence lower middle-class people in the desired direction. For these orgies and extravagances were condemned with a moral indignation which was all the more poisonous as it cloaked envy of those who embraced life unhesitatingly.

I mean the Batman Begins “controlling idea” that you put forward isn’t wrong as much as it is incomplete. That is a central idea of the film but it lacks all of the context or the complexity within it and gives a reductionist view of the ethical and moral difficulties that the film is centered on so strongly. It’s not that you are wrong, it’s that the mode of interpretation, or rather the brevity of the controlling idea creates a false vision. I find the main thematic underpinnings of the film, and the trilogy in general, to be concerning justice. Batman is a vigilante figure who tries to correct the self destructive and morally chaotic Gotham city outside of the jurisdiction and authority of the democratically elected state. However, the principle antagonist to the film, far more than the destructive organized crime groups like Falcone’s organization, is a radical, fascistic militia group who abandon faith in Gothams ability to organically self correct and decided to organize Gotham’s implosion through hallucinatory chemical weapons. So both parties have the same pursuit, with different means of carrying it out. So in essence boiling it down into the catchphrase “It’s not who you are underneath. It’s what you do that defines you” is true, but that could equally be interpreted as a call to heroism and transcending inaction. But I don’t think that’s the primary concern of the movie, because passivity is not the primary threat to Gotham, it is a threat, but a fanatical devotion to principle is what causes Gothams flirtation with oblivion. So I believe that it is not just possible, but stimulating to analyze films while trying to not over intellectualize the experience and devoid it of its emotional power. I actually think it’s necessary, not to see how smart we are or to come up with a single unchallengeable and un disposable interpretation of a film, but to also defend against propaganda as well. I think the Batman example is a great one because the major cultural fascination and obsession with superheroes and the genres natural sympathies with propaganda and fascist impulses are important to recognize. Superheroes becomes cultural icons and tend to be on the verge of worship, they are usually presented as totally altruistic and completely just, ethical discussion regarding their inherent vigilantism is practically nonexistent, and their antagonists are defeated with relish and encouraged by the audience from their immediate introduction. So examining that dichotomy in a post imperial, modern society is important. But as I said before I don’t want to forget the emotional power of a story, but cinema operates on two separate fields, there is the form of visual storytelling and there is the narrative. The form can be discussed, but in much more general terms, it’s a common saying that a picture is worth a thousand words, but a movie is 24 pictures per second for 2-3 hours. So converting the visual form into words has diminishing returns. But I see no reason why we cannot discuss and write about film narrative like you would a piece of literature. To distill the narrative on screen to a concise, well reasoned and observant piece of criticism that acknowledges the moral and ethical implications of the events and the characters behavior, recognizes the thematic content and tries to find with the film itself and the context of the time and creator of the piece the intent behind the expression. A film like 2001 can’t be reduced down to a single line of written prose, but you can write pages and pages about the ways in which Kubrick focuses on evolution, tribal conflict, artificial intelligence and the questions of the metaphysical in the age of science.

Maybe read some other Bordwells too, his books on the development of film history as a field (note: not an uncomplicated history of film, really a history on film historiography, though you will get a more sophisticated understanding of film history than most by reading it) and on the "Classical Hollywood" film production industry are both excellent.

Then, we have theoretical approaches. Film specific stuff is good but plenty of fields have theories of how culture fuctions within society which can aid in interpretation, many of which were just imported into film studies entirely. You can go in via the broader world of philosophy/linguistics/literature, you can start in film studies with something like Film Art and then tackle cultural theory work as it comes up by going through academic Reader books like The Film Studies Reader or Narrative, Apparatus, Ideology. A good academic "Reader" book is always a useful snapshot of where a field of study is, and if it's contemporary it can get you up to speed pretty quickly.

the writing thing is actually the fastest path imo. even if it's garbage at first, forcing yourself to articulate why something worked or didn't work trains you to notice things you'd otherwise just absorb passively.

one thing that helped me a lot early on: after watching something, try to identify just one specific moment that hit you and figure out *why* that moment lands. not the whole film, just one scene. the camera choice, the silence before a line, the cut. you start to realize how intentional most of it is, and then you can't stop noticing it everywhere.

also reading Ebert's Great Movies essays alongside rewatches is genuinely good. he's not academic about it but he's precise, and that combo is useful when you're building vocabulary.

I realised how little time I actually had to work on analysing a certain film and research and how I acutally valued talking about the films and the whole atmosphere and watching 5 films daily half-awake and having a beer with fellow jurors afterwards. The world around film is amazing and I strongly advise anyone passionate to get involved.

What I gathered from that experience is that more often than not when you get through some share of films in your life what is valuable stays with you without trying so hard and the most important skill is to know what to look for in a certain film and what is a waste of time. You can get a lot more value while watching the movie. If you like something about it - pursue it! read a book, watch something similar, juxtapose with another film. But truth is - it really most of the time doesn't amount to much, you just might get to enjoy yourself for a while and later enjoy a different movie more.
